highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Reduck Secures $3M to Cut AI Agent Web Tasks 3x [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 22, 2026 · 16 min read A French-American startup called Reduck has raised $3 million in a pre-seed funding round to solve a problem that has quietly become one of the biggest bottlenecks in agentic AI: what happens when the website an AI agent needs to use has no API. The round, reported by [Tech.eu](https://tech.eu/2026/10/22/reduck-secures-3m-to-make-web-automation-faster-for-ai-agents/) on October 22, 2026, was led by Daphni, with participation from Drysdale Ventures and Galion.exe. The money is going toward a product called Reduck MCP, a platform that lets AI agents discover, execute, and even create browser-automation scripts on their own, without an engineer wiring up a traditional API integration first. The timing matters. Over the past year, AI agents have moved from chatbot demos to systems that book travel, file expense reports, scrape competitor pricing, and manage CRM records on a company’s behalf. Nearly all of that work depends on software talking to other software through APIs. But most of the internet still does not expose a clean API, and a lot of enterprise software locks its most useful functions behind login screens and custom web interfaces. Reduck is betting that the gap between “agents that can reason” and “agents that can actually click buttons on a website” is where the next wave of AI infrastructure spending will land. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Reduck Actually Builds: Inside the Reduck MCP Platform Reduck’s core product, Reduck MCP, is built around the Model Context Protocol, the open standard that lets AI models call external tools in a structured way. Instead of asking a developer to write and maintain a custom integration for every target website, Reduck MCP gives an AI agent a library it can search, a way to execute an existing automation, and a way to generate a brand-new one when nothing suitable exists yet. According to the Tech.eu report, that library already contains more than 1,200 ready-to-run automation scripts spanning over 250 websites, which means an agent calling Reduck MCP is often reusing work that has already been built, tested, and hosted rather than improvising from scratch on every request. Reduck’s own site lists use cases that illustrate the idea in practice, including [building a company list and enriching it with funding and news](https://reduck.ai/use-cases/research-startups-and-funding) pulled straight from the web rather than a paid data API. That “discover, execute, create” loop is the part Reduck is pitching as its differentiator. Most browser-automation tooling built for AI agents today still asks a human to define the workflow up front: click here, type there, wait for this element to load. Reduck flips that order. The agent decides what it needs to accomplish, searches Reduck’s hosted library for a matching automation, runs it if one exists, and if nothing matches, the agent itself produces a new automation script that Reduck then hosts and executes going forward. highlights.titleZh: Dell unveils Nvidia Vera CPU offerings, launches its first Groq 3 LPU rack-scale inference solution - DCD
highlights.content: # Dell unveils Nvidia Vera CPU offerings, launches its first Groq 3 LPU rack-scale inference solution All have been purpose-built for agentic AI, Dell said Dell Technologies has expanded its Dell AI Factory with Nvidia product portfolio, adding a Vera CPU server and rack, and a rack-scale inference system built on Groq 3 Language Processing Units (LPUs), to its hardware lineup. In a statement, Dell said its AI Factory platform has surpassed 6,500 customers, up from 5,000 in the previous quarter. The Dell PowerEdge M9882 comprises 256 Nvidia Vera CPUs in a single 48U rack, allowing companies to maximize data center power and cooling capacity by separating out CPU compute from GPU clusters. Dell said the rack has been purpose-built to support agentic AI workloads, and offers orchestration, tool use, code execution and evaluation, which can run alongside GPU infrastructure for model inference. Meanwhile, the Dell PowerEdge R8822 server is an air-cooled, two-socket Nvidia Vera CPU offering that fits into standard 19-inch rack environments. Like its rack-scale counterpart, the R8822 has also been optimized for agentic AI workloads and can run reinforcement learning, data processing, and analytics, with support for up to four double-wide GPUs to accelerate AI and compute-intensive tasks. Finally, Dell has launched the PowerEdge XE9810, the first offering from the company to feature Groq 3 LPUs. Featuring 16 direct-liquid-cooled compute trays, Dell did not provide details on the number of LPUs per tray, but said that the server functions as “an ideal disaggregated complement to existing GPU clusters,” purpose-built for the high-throughput demands of production agentic AI. “Enterprises used to think about AI infrastructure as an IT budget question, but that's changed,” said Michael Dell, CEO of Dell Technologies. “AI infrastructure is no longer a cost center. It's a value creation center. Companies are expanding and reallocating budgets because AI infrastructure drives growth, productivity and competitive advantage. Together with Nvidia, we are giving enterprises the integrated platforms they need to move agentic AI from experimentation to results, on infrastructure they own and control.” The Dell PowerEdge R8822 will be available this month, with the M9882 and XE9810 coming in Q1 2027.

highlights.content: SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 22, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The research explores advances in LLM training, adaptive reasoning, and reinforcement learning. Ten papers involving researchers from MemoraX AI’s founding research team and its academic and industry collaborators have been accepted to the 2026 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), one of the leading international conferences in artificial intelligence and machine learning. The research spans large language model (LLM) post-training, inference optimization, adaptive reasoning, and online reinforcement learning. Across these areas, the work explores how AI systems can learn more reliably, allocate computational resources more effectively, and make better decisions in complex environments. NeurIPS 2026 will take place December 6–12 in Sydney, Australia, with satellite events in Atlanta, Georgia, and Paris, France, from December 9–13. Advancing AI Learning, Reasoning, and Decision-Making As AI agents take on increasingly complex and long-running tasks, researchers face fundamental challenges: making model training more reliable, aligning training objectives with actual inference performance, allocating reasoning resources more effectively, and developing robust decision-making strategies for complex environments. MemoraX AI is building next-generation AI memory infrastructure while pursuing research in memory modeling, reinforcement learning, and agent systems. Its research explores how memory can move beyond information storage and retrieval to become a learnable capability that helps agents retain context, manage information, and apply accumulated experience to future tasks. The company’s work spans text memory, work and coding memory, and multimodal memory. For developers building AI applications, Memory API supports memory writing, search, updates, and deletion. MemoraX Code, the company’s persistent-memory tool for coding agents, helps agents retain repository structure, architectural decisions, coding preferences, and debugging experience across sessions and agents. The underlying technical challenge is how to make memory itself learnable, enabling systems to determine what to retain, when to update or retrieve information, and how to turn historical interactions into reusable experience. Four Representative Papers Four representative papers from the NeurIPS 2026 selections illustrate different approaches to improving AI learning, reasoning, and decision-making. 1. Beyond Correctness: Robustness-Driven Evolutionary Self-Training for Large Language Models Research focus: LLM post-training and reasoning reliability A correct answer does not necessarily indicate a reliable reasoning process. This paper introduces TREST, a robustness-driven evolutionary self-training framework that evaluates the stability of reasoning paths under sampling perturbations and prioritizes more robust trajectories for training. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, TREST achieved an average accuracy of 49.83%, outperforming the GRPO and Iterative RFT baselines in the reported experiments. The work offers an approach to improving the reliability of LLM reasoning by considering not only whether a solution is correct, but also whether the reasoning strategy remains effective under variation. 2. The Mirage of Optimizing Training Policies: Monotonic Inference Policies as the Real Objective for LLM Reinforcement Learning Research focus: Reinforcement learning and inference optimization Improvements during training do not always translate into better performance when a model is deployed. This paper examines inconsistencies between training and inference in LLM reinforcement learning, where improvements in a training policy may not translate into better performance from the policy used at inference time. AI agents are systems that complete tasks, use tools and interact with websites, often autonomously and with limited human oversight. As part of the call for evidence, the ICO’s Director of Technology Regulation said: “the fact AI agents act with autonomy is not an excuse for poor compliance.” The call is built around six themes, each being an area where the ICO found organisations struggling with a lack of clarity on how to apply data protection laws to agentic AI and on which the ICO sets out its current expectations. The call for evidence closes on 20 November 2026, and the responses will shape future ICO guidance and its forthcoming statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making. In this blog post, we look at what the ICO says it expects from organisations using AI agents across the six themes and set out practical steps they can take now. **Security: control what the agent can do** Agents can act autonomously without direction or sign-off from a human at each step. The ICO points to an example of an agent that might retrieve external information and update an internal database on its own. The ICO states that this raises “the risk that security failures or malicious instructions” could “spread across connected systems”, and expects the level of autonomy given to agents to be a “deliberate” design choice, backed by guardrails, permissions and approval thresholds proportionate to the risk of what an agent can do with personal data. This means that existing security principles under the UK GDPR will continue to apply to agents, but relevant controls must be designed by organisations to account for what an agent can access and do. Measures such as least-privilege access, limits on tool use and human approval for high-risk actions are cited by the ICO as emerging approaches to manage agents (and they will be familiar to many organisations), but the ICO is clear that they must actively govern what an agent can access, which tools it uses and what actions it takes. The ICO states that organisations will need “a clear way to identify when an agent is operating” to enable appropriate guardrails, and introduces a concept of agentic “ownership”, suggesting that deployers of agents register each agent to an owner, and give it a set purpose and set of permissions and capabilities. **Transparency: explaining a moving target** An agent may gather information from a device, internal systems, screenshots or external tools. The processing can vary extensively, and sources and recipients of data can change every time its workflow runs. AI Agents.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Reduck Secures $3M to Cut AI Agent Web Tasks 3x [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 22, 2026 · 16 min read A French-American startup called Reduck has raised $3 million in a pre-seed funding round to solve a problem that has quietly become one of the biggest bottlenecks in agentic AI: what happens when the website an AI agent needs to use has no API. The round, reported by [Tech.eu](https://tech.eu/2026/10/22/reduck-secures-3m-to-make-web-automation-faster-for-ai-agents/) on October 22, 2026, was led by Daphni, with participation from Drysdale Ventures and Galion.exe. The money is going toward a product called Reduck MCP, a platform that lets AI agents discover, execute, and even create browser-automation scripts on their own, without an engineer wiring up a traditional API integration first. The timing matters. Over the past year, AI agents have moved from chatbot demos to systems that book travel, file expense reports, scrape competitor pricing, and manage CRM records on a company’s behalf. Nearly all of that work depends on software talking to other software through APIs. But most of the internet still does not expose a clean API, and a lot of enterprise software locks its most useful functions behind login screens and custom web interfaces. Reduck is betting that the gap between “agents that can reason” and “agents that can actually click buttons on a website” is where the next wave of AI infrastructure spending will land. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Reduck Actually Builds: Inside the Reduck MCP Platform Reduck’s core product, Reduck MCP, is built around the Model Context Protocol, the open standard that lets AI models call external tools in a structured way. Instead of asking a developer to write and maintain a custom integration for every target website, Reduck MCP gives an AI agent a library it can search, a way to execute an existing automation, and a way to generate a brand-new one when nothing suitable exists yet. According to the Tech.eu report, that library already contains more than 1,200 ready-to-run automation scripts spanning over 250 websites, which means an agent calling Reduck MCP is often reusing work that has already been built, tested, and hosted rather than improvising from scratch on every request. Reduck’s own site lists use cases that illustrate the idea in practice, including [building a company list and enriching it with funding and news](https://reduck.ai/use-cases/research-startups-and-funding) pulled straight from the web rather than a paid data API. That “discover, execute, create” loop is the part Reduck is pitching as its differentiator. Most browser-automation tooling built for AI agents today still asks a human to define the workflow up front: click here, type there, wait for this element to load. Reduck flips that order. The agent decides what it needs to accomplish, searches Reduck’s hosted library for a matching automation, runs it if one exists, and if nothing matches, the agent itself produces a new automation script that Reduck then hosts and executes going forward. AI agents are systems that complete tasks, use tools and interact with websites, often autonomously and with limited human oversight. As part of the call for evidence, the ICO’s Director of Technology Regulation said: “the fact AI agents act with autonomy is not an excuse for poor compliance.” The call is built around six themes, each being an area where the ICO found organisations struggling with a lack of clarity on how to apply data protection laws to agentic AI and on which the ICO sets out its current expectations. The call for evidence closes on 20 November 2026, and the responses will shape future ICO guidance and its forthcoming statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making. In this blog post, we look at what the ICO says it expects from organisations using AI agents across the six themes and set out practical steps they can take now. **Security: control what the agent can do** Agents can act autonomously without direction or sign-off from a human at each step. The ICO points to an example of an agent that might retrieve external information and update an internal database on its own. The ICO states that this raises “the risk that security failures or malicious instructions” could “spread across connected systems”, and expects the level of autonomy given to agents to be a “deliberate” design choice, backed by guardrails, permissions and approval thresholds proportionate to the risk of what an agent can do with personal data. This means that existing security principles under the UK GDPR will continue to apply to agents, but relevant controls must be designed by organisations to account for what an agent can access and do. Measures such as least-privilege access, limits on tool use and human approval for high-risk actions are cited by the ICO as emerging approaches to manage agents (and they will be familiar to many organisations), but the ICO is clear that they must actively govern what an agent can access, which tools it uses and what actions it takes. The ICO states that organisations will need “a clear way to identify when an agent is operating” to enable appropriate guardrails, and introduces a concept of agentic “ownership”, suggesting that deployers of agents register each agent to an owner, and give it a set purpose and set of permissions and capabilities. **Transparency: explaining a moving target** An agent may gather information from a device, internal systems, screenshots or external tools. It may then share that information with other agents or third parties, send emails or make purchases. The processing can vary extensively, and sources and recipients of data can change every time its workflow runs. AI Agents.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Progress adds Teams app & Smart Agent to RAG platform](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/22/john_yang_progress_2021-story-322167.webp) [LLMs](https://itbrief.asia/tag/large-language-models) [AI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/artificial-intelligence) [Agentic AI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/ai-agents) # Progress adds Teams app & Smart Agent to RAG platform Fri, 23rd Oct 2026 (Today) [![Sofiah Nichole Salivio](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNywicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--3f3cbcdb3f86206827b894ccc07566b24a1d49e6/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/unnamed%20(2).webp) SOFIAH NICHOLE SALIVIO News Editor](/author/sofiah-nichole-salivio) Progress Software has added new features to its Agentic RAG platform, expanding how it ingests, retrieves and delivers content for AI tools. The release includes a native Microsoft Teams app, a Smart Agent for multistep retrieval and a WordPress plugin for content ingestion. The additions are intended to help organisations use existing business knowledge across AI agents and large language models without rebuilding current deployments. The platform is built around what Progress calls a shared Agentic Knowledge Layer, which connects enterprise information to AI-driven experiences. The latest version combines pre-ingested content stored in a governed Knowledge Box with access to live business systems and web sources through native Model Context Protocol support in the Smart Agent. The approach targets a common challenge for companies extending AI beyond basic chat functions. As businesses deploy agents that can plan, retrieve information and act across multiple systems, engineering teams often have to build custom orchestration logic for every source an agent needs to access. Progress said agents that rely only on pre-indexed content can return incomplete or outdated responses. Employees may also still need to move between applications to find information, limiting adoption and weakening returns on AI spending. John Yang, Vice President, APJ, at Progress Software, framed the announcement against wider business pressures in the region. "Organisations across Asia Pacific are navigating rapid growth, evolving customer expectations and increasing operational complexity. AI has the potential to help address all three, but only when it can draw on the knowledge that already exists across the business. We believe the next phase of AI adoption will be defined less by the models themselves and more by how effectively organisations can put their knowledge to work," said Yang. **Teams integration** One part of the update is a Teams app available through the Microsoft Store. Progress said it brings source-cited AI responses into Teams chats and channels, allowing employees to access internal knowledge within a collaboration tool they already use. The Teams integration keeps existing permissions and governance controls in place. That means businesses can surface AI-driven responses in day-to-day workflows without requiring staff to leave Teams to search other systems. **Multistep retrieval** The new Smart Agent is designed to break a query into sub-questions, retrieve information from a Knowledge Box, MCP-connected applications and web sources, then assess whether enough information has been gathered. According to Progress, this process can help organisations answer more complex questions that span several systems. The feature also addresses a technical challenge in enterprise AI deployments. LLMs.content: SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 22, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The research explores advances in LLM training, adaptive reasoning, and reinforcement learning. Ten papers involving researchers from MemoraX AI’s founding research team and its academic and industry collaborators have been accepted to the 2026 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), one of the leading international conferences in artificial intelligence and machine learning. The research spans large language model (LLM) post-training, inference optimization, adaptive reasoning, and online reinforcement learning. Across these areas, the work explores how AI systems can learn more reliably, allocate computational resources more effectively, and make better decisions in complex environments. NeurIPS 2026 will take place December 6–12 in Sydney, Australia, with satellite events in Atlanta, Georgia, and Paris, France, from December 9–13. Advancing AI Learning, Reasoning, and Decision-Making As AI agents take on increasingly complex and long-running tasks, researchers face fundamental challenges: making model training more reliable, aligning training objectives with actual inference performance, allocating reasoning resources more effectively, and developing robust decision-making strategies for complex environments. MemoraX AI is building next-generation AI memory infrastructure while pursuing research in memory modeling, reinforcement learning, and agent systems. Its research explores how memory can move beyond information storage and retrieval to become a learnable capability that helps agents retain context, manage information, and apply accumulated experience to future tasks. The company’s work spans text memory, work and coding memory, and multimodal memory. For developers building AI applications, Memory API supports memory writing, search, updates, and deletion. MemoraX Code, the company’s persistent-memory tool for coding agents, helps agents retain repository structure, architectural decisions, coding preferences, and debugging experience across sessions and agents. The underlying technical challenge is how to make memory itself learnable, enabling systems to determine what to retain, when to update or retrieve information, and how to turn historical interactions into reusable experience. Four Representative Papers Four representative papers from the NeurIPS 2026 selections illustrate different approaches to improving AI learning, reasoning, and decision-making. 1. Beyond Correctness: Robustness-Driven Evolutionary Self-Training for Large Language Models Research focus: LLM post-training and reasoning reliability A correct answer does not necessarily indicate a reliable reasoning process. This paper introduces TREST, a robustness-driven evolutionary self-training framework that evaluates the stability of reasoning paths under sampling perturbations and prioritizes more robust trajectories for training. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, TREST achieved an average accuracy of 49.83%, outperforming the GRPO and Iterative RFT baselines in the reported experiments. The work offers an approach to improving the reliability of LLM reasoning by considering not only whether a solution is correct, but also whether the reasoning strategy remains effective under variation. 2. The Mirage of Optimizing Training Policies: Monotonic Inference Policies as the Real Objective for LLM Reinforcement Learning Research focus: Reinforcement learning and inference optimization Improvements during training do not always translate into better performance when a model is deployed. This paper examines inconsistencies between training and inference in LLM reinforcement learning, where improvements in a training policy may not translate into better performance from the policy used at inference time. The tool aims to help developers detect behavior changes in large language model APIs.* **Martingale introduces Raven Alpha for model drift detection** PALO ALTO, US — October 22, 2026 — Martingale, a data infrastructure and analytics company focused on artificial intelligence, announced on Tuesday the launch of Raven Alpha, a novel method for detecting drift in AI models. The company said Raven Alpha ranks first among model drift detection approaches in independent evaluations. The announcement was made by co-founders Arjun Hans, Veenu Damarla, and Jayden Ishihara, who are computer science students at Carnegie Mellon University. ![A blue, geometric origami bird flies across a black background, representing the Raven Alpha model.](https://prnow.io/uploads/press-releases/Codex_Image_Sep_24_2026_11_14_57_PM_mvjrd6ue_61069ea1.jpg) ![A blue, geometric origami bird flies across a black background, representing the Raven Alpha model.](https://prnow.io/uploads/press-releases/Codex_Image_Sep_24_2026_11_14_57_PM_mvjrd6ue_61069ea1.jpg) Model drift occurs when an AI model’s behavior changes over time, often due to updates or shifts in underlying data. For developers building products on large language model APIs from providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic, undetected drift can cause applications to fail or produce inconsistent results. Martingale’s method is designed to identify such changes before they affect end users. **Founders combine academic research with practical focus** Hans, Damarla, and Ishihara developed Raven Alpha while studying at Carnegie Mellon. According to the company, the team’s approach outperforms established drift detection techniques in head-to-head comparisons. The founders have not disclosed the specific benchmarks used, but they said the results have been validated through internal testing and will be submitted for peer review. Martingale is positioning Raven Alpha as a tool for enterprises and developers who rely on third-party AI APIs. The company said the method can be integrated into existing monitoring pipelines and provides early warnings when model behavior deviates from expected patterns. **Early access and availability** Raven Alpha is currently available in a limited early access program. Martingale plans to release a commercial version later this year, with pricing to be announced. The company said it is working with several design partners to refine the product and gather feedback from production environments. The launch comes as businesses increasingly depend on AI models for critical functions, raising the stakes for reliability and consistency. Martingale’s entry into the drift detection market adds a new option for organizations seeking to maintain oversight of third-party AI systems. **About Martingale** Martingale is a data infrastructure and analytics company specializing in AI model monitoring and drift detection. LLMs.title: Google Chrysalis: 3 Timescales, 5 Guardrails [2026]
LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Google Chrysalis: 3 Timescales, 5 Guardrails [2026] ![Priya Anand](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/panand.webp) [Priya Anand](https://shattered.io/author/panand/) Updated Oct 22, 2026 · 15 min read Google Cloud published a research reference architecture on October 22, 2026 that shows how **self-evolving AI agents** can patch a live incident while staying inside hard security limits. The Google Developers Blog post, [Architecting Governed, Self-Evolving AI Agents on the Gemini platform](https://developers.googleblog.com/architecting-governed-self-evolving-ai-agents-on-gemini-agent-platform), names the design Project Chrysalis and builds it on the Gemini platform and the Agent Development Kit (ADK). The pitch is easy to say and hard to build. An agent diagnoses an outage, writes a mitigation tool, verifies it, mounts it, and learns from the result. Every step sits behind signatures, policy checks, and a human gate. Google describes the work as a research reference architecture and an interactive application, so nobody should read it as a product that shipped today. Still, the post lands at a busy moment for Google’s agent stack. The company has spent the fall pushing the Gemini family forward, and we followed the [Gemini 4 Argon rollout into AI Mode](https://shattered.io/gemini-4-argon-ai-mode-19-countries-2026/) only days ago. Chrysalis shows what Google thinks **governed AI agents** should look like once models like that run production operations. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Google Cloud Published on October 22 The Google Developers Blog post presents Chrysalis as a worked example, not a feature announcement. According to the post, the architecture runs on the Gemini platform (the post’s URL calls it the Gemini Agent Platform) and ADK, and Google’s own summary of the post also lists BigQuery as part of the stack. It ships with an interactive application so readers can watch the agent behavior instead of only reading about it. Google lists five capabilities for the design: * Distributed root-cause diagnosis across the tiers of a live system * Self-patching through synthesized and verified mitigation tools * Self-critique of the agent’s own actions * Cryptographically signed operational memory * Dynamic changes to the multi-agent hierarchy, with human sign-off The security side gets equal billing. Google names Model Armor, Google Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS), Binary Authorization, the Open Policy Agent (OPA) Policy Controller, and Dual-Custody Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) governance as the components that keep the agent inside its limits. We break each one down below. Just as important is what the post leaves out. It gives no price, no performance benchmark, no deployment date, and no customer list. Treat everything in this article as a description of a design, not a measured result. ## Project Chrysalis in Plain Terms Think of Chrysalis as an on-call engineer that can write code, with a security team standing behind it at every keystroke. The agent watches a failing system, forms a diagnosis, and builds a small tool to stop the damage. Then it asks whether its own action helped or hurt. ### The incident-response use case Google’s example centers on outages that span a cache tier and a database tier. Per the post, the agent diagnoses the root cause across those tiers in real time. It then synthesizes an executable mitigation tool, verifies it, and mounts it into live server middleware. That last step is the bold one. The agent does not just recommend a fix to a human. It ships a patch into a running system. To keep that from turning reckless, the design scores its own work. LLMs.title: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up | TechCrunch
LLMs.titleZh: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up | TechCrunch
LLMs.content: OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company. TypeSafe’s Jev model created a category for deep learning models that act as super classifiers: Given a set of options, they can quickly make choices and offer a confidence rating in their decision. Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost. Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost. “The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.” Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically. In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness. Still, it’s not clear exactly what makes a good decision model, other than “it works for you” — optimization across intelligence, cost, calibration, and speed seems to differ by workload. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model. Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1. The latest Jev model remains competitive on both indices, in seventh and third, with OpenAI’s Decision Model falling eighth and fourteenth, respectively. However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter. The most fun Jev benchmark, however, is JevMan, a benchmark where decision models play PacMan; the latest Jev model tops that ranking. Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions. At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.” Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well. Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new uses cases—”Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?” As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who predicted that a cheap commodity only gets more ubiquitous. Or, as Handa puts it, “the crazy set of use cases”...

Wuhan Zhiyue Chuangda Technology adopts the dual-engine architecture of "Intelligent Central Base + AI Development Framework", which shortens the delivery cycle of enterprise customized AI systems from several months to one week. At present, its products have expanded from the development platform to desktop terminals, all-in-one machines and C-end scientific research applications. In July 2025, Wuhan Zhiyue Chuangda Technology Co., Ltd. launched ZAI (Zero to AI), an enterprise-level one-stop AI agent development platform. According to the team, enterprises can complete the development and launch of business intelligence based on this platform in as fast as only one week. Tang Shengwu, founder of Zhiyue Chuangda, has 15 years of experience in the IT industry, and has served as architect, technical director, senior engineer and other positions. The core team is composed of a number of technical experts from well-known technology enterprises. The project started technical R&D in January 2025. The team spent half a year polishing the first version and continued to iterate afterwards. At present, it has completed the layout on four product lines: B-end platform, desktop office, software-hardware integration and C-end scientific research assistant. ## **I. Three Thresholds for Enterprise AI Implementation: Technology, Cost and Security** The capabilities of large models have been rapidly popularized in the past three years, but on the enterprise side, there is still a considerable gap between "being able to use AI" and "using AI well". An available agent involves multiple links such as model invocation, knowledge base construction, tool orchestration, permission and security. It is difficult for enterprises without AI engineering experience to connect these links on their own. Second, the implementation cycle is long. The traditional customized development from demand sorting to system launch is often calculated in months, which cannot meet the timeliness requirement of business. Third, it is difficult to balance cost and security. Building a self-owned team requires large investment, while standardized SaaS products are difficult to match the personalized business processes and private data requirements of enterprises. As a result, many enterprises' AI attempts remain at the single-point pilot stage and are difficult to enter the core business process. "Either spend a lot of money on self-development, or make do with general products". This mismatch is exactly the market gap targeted by Zhiyue Chuangda's ZAI platform. ## **II. Open Source AI.title: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA | WIRED
Open Source AI.titleZh: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA | WIRED
Open Source AI.content: # Hugging Face’s New AI Model Lets You Chat With DNA The AI platform Hugging Face on Thursday released a new open model for understanding DNA that can run locally on a laptop. Developed in collaboration with researchers at Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, the model is trained on genomic sequences and natural language so that people can ask questions about the effects of DNA changes on gene activity and health and get conversational answers in return. Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face, says the tool is meant to help researchers design new drugs and genetic therapies, and it could potentially aid patients in interpreting their own genomes. “We've unlocked a new capability in language models, which is fundamentally about being able to chat with DNA,” he says of the new model, dubbed Carbon-X. Using natural language means even nontechnical users “can actually ask questions about DNA that wouldn't be accessible through any other tool.” Known as essentially GitHub for AI models, Hugging Face provides a library of readymade AI tools and a platform for running primarily open-weight and open-source AI applications for developers, researchers, businesses, and people who want to experiment with AI without building everything from scratch. In September, Nvidia agreed to acquire the company for nearly $13 billion. (Hugging Face was also at the center of a major hack by OpenAI’s models earlier this year.) DNA is more like computer code than natural language. Instead of 0s and 1s, though, it uses As, Cs, Gs, and Ts to encode information. A human genome contains 6 billion of these letters. While the human genome has been sequenced end to end, scientists still don’t understand how most of it works. Now, AI models are helping researchers decipher some of those mysteries. Last year, Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome, which predicts the effects of DNA sequences and genetic mutations but does so in a numeric format. It also requires more compute power. Evo 2, a model developed by the Arc Institute and Nvidia, along with academic partners, speaks the language of DNA and can generate entire genomes from scratch. Carbon-X integrates both DNA and natural language in a conversational interface. Think of it like a ChatGPT for DNA. The team started with an existing language model and expanded its vocabulary to read DNA in groups of six letters. They then continued training on 300 billion chunks of data, or tokens, that combined DNA sequences, English text, and examples linking DNA to biological descriptions. The DNA sequences came from mammals (including humans), other vertebrates, invertebrates, plants, fungi, and protozoa. Tunstall says the team didn’t train the model on viruses because they didn’t want it to be used for potentially dangerous applications. Users won’t be able to upload full human genomes. The model was trained to be able to ingest DNA sequences of roughly 50,000 base pairs, so users will only be able to query small parts of the genome at a time. One of the ways scientists could use Carbon-X is to help understand whether a genetic mutation is benign or disease-causing, a key step in developing a targeted drug or genetic therapy. If an intervention targets the wrong mutation, it could be totally ineffective or, worse, cause unintended harm. Researchers face restrictions when it comes to uploading identifiable or sensitive patient data to frontier AI models, so Tunstall says his team intentionally designed a small model with 14 billion parameters. That will allow it to run locally on the user’s hardware, rather than rely on cloud-based models. No data is sent to Hugging Face or any other company, he says. The developers of Carbon-X caution that they haven’t validated the model yet with actual wet lab experiments, so they can’t say how accurate its predictions are.

Infra & Chips.titleZh: Dell unveils Nvidia Vera CPU offerings, launches its first Groq 3 LPU rack-scale inference solution - DCD
Infra & Chips.content: # Dell unveils Nvidia Vera CPU offerings, launches its first Groq 3 LPU rack-scale inference solution All have been purpose-built for agentic AI, Dell said Dell Technologies has expanded its Dell AI Factory with Nvidia product portfolio, adding a Vera CPU server and rack, and a rack-scale inference system built on Groq 3 Language Processing Units (LPUs), to its hardware lineup. In a statement, Dell said its AI Factory platform has surpassed 6,500 customers, up from 5,000 in the previous quarter. The Dell PowerEdge M9882 comprises 256 Nvidia Vera CPUs in a single 48U rack, allowing companies to maximize data center power and cooling capacity by separating out CPU compute from GPU clusters. Dell said the rack has been purpose-built to support agentic AI workloads, and offers orchestration, tool use, code execution and evaluation, which can run alongside GPU infrastructure for model inference. Meanwhile, the Dell PowerEdge R8822 server is an air-cooled, two-socket Nvidia Vera CPU offering that fits into standard 19-inch rack environments. Like its rack-scale counterpart, the R8822 has also been optimized for agentic AI workloads and can run reinforcement learning, data processing, and analytics, with support for up to four double-wide GPUs to accelerate AI and compute-intensive tasks. Finally, Dell has launched the PowerEdge XE9810, the first offering from the company to feature Groq 3 LPUs. Featuring 16 direct-liquid-cooled compute trays, Dell did not provide details on the number of LPUs per tray, but said that the server functions as “an ideal disaggregated complement to existing GPU clusters,” purpose-built for the high-throughput demands of production agentic AI. “Enterprises used to think about AI infrastructure as an IT budget question, but that's changed,” said Michael Dell, CEO of Dell Technologies. “AI infrastructure is no longer a cost center. It's a value creation center. Companies are expanding and reallocating budgets because AI infrastructure drives growth, productivity and competitive advantage. Together with Nvidia, we are giving enterprises the integrated platforms they need to move agentic AI from experimentation to results, on infrastructure they own and control.” The Dell PowerEdge R8822 will be available this month, with the M9882 and XE9810 coming in Q1 2027.

[Nvidia](https://www.nvidia.com) CEO Jensen Huang just diagnosed the AI infrastructure boom's growing pain: too much demand, not enough money. In a Thursday interview with [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/22/nvidia-jensen-huang-neocloud-demand-capital.html), Huang said customer appetite for neocloud services has gone "off the charts," but the capital required to meet that demand simply isn't flowing fast enough. The neocloud sector—AI-native infrastructure providers like CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, and others building massive GPU clusters—represents Nvidia's fastest-growing customer segment. These companies don't just resell compute; they're architecting the backbone for the next generation of AI applications, from large language model training to real-time inference at scale. But building that infrastructure requires billions in upfront capital for chips, data centers, and power infrastructure. The new practice focuses on the infrastructure required to support AI training and inference workloads, including high-speed networking, GPU servers, storage systems, cooling technologies and automated infrastructure monitoring. The offering targets organizations building private AI computing capacity within their own facilities or through colocation providers, where specialized networking and computing requirements can create challenges for traditional enterprise IT environments. Innovorbs will provide infrastructure design, implementation and ongoing management services, including support for high-performance GPU clusters using 400-gigabit and 800-gigabit Ethernet networks. The company said its approach integrates networking, computing, storage and facilities engineering to address the performance demands of large-scale AI workloads. Unlike conventional enterprise applications, AI training systems frequently require substantial data transfers between GPUs operating across multiple servers. These workloads can be sensitive to network congestion, latency and packet loss, making specialized networking infrastructure an important component of GPU cluster performance. Innovorbs’ new practice includes the design of high-performance back-end networks using Remote Direct Memory Access over Converged Ethernet, or RoCEv2, a technology that enables efficient data transfers between computing systems. The company will support networking technologies and equipment from NVIDIA, Arista, Cisco and Juniper, including NVIDIA Spectrum-X, Cisco Nexus and Juniper QFX platforms. For AI deployments requiring InfiniBand networking, Innovorbs will also support NVIDIA Quantum InfiniBand environments using NDR and XDR technologies. Its engineering services include network congestion management, adaptive routing and specialized network architectures designed to maintain performance as GPU clusters expand. Innovorbs will validate communication between GPUs using technologies such as NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) and GPUDirect RDMA, which support high-speed data transfers across AI computing systems. The practice also addresses connections between GPUs within individual servers through NVIDIA NVLink and NVSwitch technologies. Beyond GPU-to-GPU networking, Innovorbs will design front-end and storage networks using technologies including BGP EVPN-VXLAN and NVMe over Fabrics. The storage component will support high-performance data access through NVMe/TCP, NVMe/RoCE and GPUDirect Storage, alongside parallel file systems such as Lustre, WEKA and VAST. These systems are intended to help AI workloads access large datasets while reducing potential bottlenecks between computing and storage infrastructure. On the computing side, Innovorbs will support GPU platforms including NVIDIA HGX and DGX, AMD Instinct and GPU servers from Dell, Supermicro and Hewlett Packard Enterprise.
